question: In Figure 6D-1, how is the preferred STOP/SLOW paddle positioned to stop traffic?
model_answer: Direct Answer: To stop traffic with the preferred method, the flagger faces road users and holds the STOP paddle face toward them in a stationary position with the arm extended horizontally away from the body, while the free arm is raised with the palm above shoulder level toward approaching traffic. Figure 6D-1 illustrates this posture with the R1-1 STOP face on a staff at least 18 inches wide. Standards (mandatory): - "To stop road users, the flagger shall face road users and aim the STOP paddle face toward road users in a stationary position with the arm extended horizontally away from the body. The free arm shall be held with the palm of the hand above shoulder level toward approaching traffic." Guidance (recommended): - "The STOP/SLOW paddle (see Figure 6D-1 and Table 6G-1) should be the primary and preferred hand-signaling device because the STOP/SLOW paddle gives road users more positive guidance than red flags." Support: - "The optimum method of displaying a STOP or SLOW message is to place the STOP/SLOW paddle on a rigid staff that is tall enough that when the end of the staff is resting on the ground, the message is high enough to be seen by approaching or stopped traffic." - "The use of paddles and flags by flaggers is illustrated in Figure 6D-1." Visual evidence: - [Image 1] Figure 6D-1 shows the "TO STOP TRAFFIC" preferred method: the flagger holds the R1-1 STOP paddle (18 inches minimum width) stationary on a staff with one arm, while the free arm is raised with the palm facing approaching traffic above shoulder level. - [Image 2] shows the same Figure 6D-1 layout on the full page, contrasting the preferred paddle method with the emergency-only flag method for stopping traffic. Citations: - Section 6D.05 Standard §3 (p.785) - Section 6D.02 Guidance §1 (p.783) - Section 6D.02 Support §5 (p.783) - Section 6D.05 Support §1 (p.785) - Figure 6D-1 (p.784)
gold_answer: The flagger faces traffic and holds the STOP face toward road users with the paddle in a stationary position and the free arm raised with the palm toward traffic.
